title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: Given an array of positive integers, decide whether it can be split into two groups whose sums are equal. Every element must go into exactly one of the two groups.
realWorld: Two-way load balancing: dividing a batch of jobs between two workers so both finish at the same moment, or splitting a set of invoice lines into two payments of equal value. The decision version is the classic NP-complete partition problem; the DP below is pseudo-polynomial, which is what makes it practical whenever the totals are small.

examples.explanation: Total is 22, so each side must reach 11: [11] against [1,5,5].
Total is 11, an odd number, so no split can halve it. One test rules the whole input out before any table is built.

Total is 12 and each side would need 6, but no subset sums to 6 — the reachable sums are 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 12. An even total is necessary and not sufficient, which is the case a parity-only check gets wrong.

constraints: Each element belongs to exactly one group
sum(nums) <= 20000, which is what makes the pseudo-polynomial table feasible

bruteForce.idea: Enumerate every subset, add it up, and check whether it equals half the total.
bruteForce.whySlow: 2^n subsets: a million at n = 20, a billion at n = 30, and the array may hold 200 numbers. The repeated work is the question 'can the remaining items make up what is still missing?' — its answer depends only on how much is still missing, not on which items produced the running total. With values up to 100 and 200 items there are at most a few thousand distinct 'amount still missing' values, yet the enumeration re-answers each of them for every one of the exponentially many item combinations that reach it.

patternIdentification: Items taken at most once, and a question about which totals are reachable — that is 0/1 knapsack with the value dimension deleted, leaving only feasibility. Two things follow immediately. First, an odd total can never split evenly, so return false before allocating anything; the halving is only meaningful when total is even. Second, the state is dp[s] = 'can some subset of the items processed so far sum to exactly s', the recurrence per item is dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - num] (leave the item, or take it and cover the rest with the earlier items), and the base case is dp[0] = true because the empty subset makes zero. The detail that decides whether the code is right is the loop direction when the 2-D table is flattened to one array: the capacity loop must run DOWNWARDS. dp[s - num] must still describe the world before this item was offered; sweeping upwards reads a cell this same item has already written, which silently allows one item to be used twice. That single rule is the most-missed detail in every knapsack variant, counting or feasibility alike.

optimized.idea: After the odd-total exit, run a feasibility knapsack with capacity half the total. One boolean array, items in the outer loop, capacity descending in the inner loop. The moment dp[half] turns true the answer is settled, so the loop can stop early.
code: if ((total & 1) == 1) return false;   // an odd total cannot be halved — exit before any work
boolean[] dp = new boolean[half + 1];   // index 0..half inclusive
dp[0] = true;   // the empty subset reaches 0
for (int s = half; s >= num; s--) {   // DOWNWARDS: dp[s - num] must predate this item

commonMistakes: Sweeping the capacity loop upwards (for s = num; s <= half; s++). dp[s - num] already includes the current item, so one item can be spent twice: [3,3,2] reaches 4 by using the 2 twice and the function returns true where the correct answer is false.

Dropping the odd-total early exit and relying on half = total / 2 with integer division. On [1,2,3,5] the total of 11 becomes a half of 5, a subset summing to 5 exists ({5} or {2,3}), and the function returns true instead of false.

Allocating boolean[half] instead of boolean[half + 1]. The capacity axis runs from 0 to half inclusive, so the one cell that holds the answer is missing — [1,5,11,5] throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at s = 11 on the very first item.
